# nanoGPT

> Train or finetune a GPT language model with two short Python files: a 330-line model and a 336-line training loop.

**496/496 citations verified** against the code at `3adf61e` on 2026-11-06. Generated by [Onramp](https://github.com/SanyamWadhwa07/onramp).

nanoGPT is Andrej Karpathy's minimal code for training GPT-style language models, released under the MIT License [`LICENSE:1-3`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/LICENSE#L1-L3). `model.py` defines the whole GPT, `train.py` trains it, and `sample.py` generates text from the result. The same code trains a baby Shakespeare model in about 3 minutes on one GPU or reproduces GPT-2 (124M) in about 4 days on eight A100s [`README.md:13`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L13). Since November 2025 the README sends new users to its successor, nanochat, and keeps this repo up "for posterity" [`README.md:9`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L9).

*In one picture:* nanoGPT is a recipe card, not a bakery. One card (`model.py`) says what the bread is made of, another (`train.py`) says how to knead and bake it, and the same two cards bake a bun (a 10.65M-parameter Shakespeare model in minutes) or a wedding cake (GPT-2 124M over 4 days on 8 GPUs). The comparison stops at everything around the oven: a bakery has quality checks, packaging and delivery, and nanoGPT has no tests, no evaluation suite and no serving code.

## The gist

### What nanoGPT is and what it is for

*core · 4 min*

**In short:** nanoGPT is two short files that build and train a GPT, plus small scripts that prepare text and generate from the result. The same code trains a 10.65M-parameter Shakespeare model on a laptop or reproduces GPT-2 (124M) on eight GPUs.

By the end of this stop you know what is in the repo and what each part is for.

A **GPT** is a neural network that reads a stretch of text and predicts what comes next. Train it on enough text and it writes plausible new text, one piece at a time. nanoGPT is Andrej Karpathy's minimal version of that idea, written to be fast enough for real runs. The README calls it a rewrite of his teaching repo minGPT that "prioritizes teeth over education" [`README.md:13`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L13): simple, but tuned to actually reproduce GPT-2.

The whole system is four kinds of file:

- `data/<name>/prepare.py` turns raw text into a file of integers.
- `model.py` (330 lines) defines the network, the class `GPT` [`model.py:118-133`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L118-L133).
- `train.py` (336 lines) trains it and saves `ckpt.pt`.
- `sample.py` loads `ckpt.pt` and writes new text.

Settings live in `config/` as tiny Python files. The one this guide uses most is the "baby GPT": 6 layers, 6 attention heads, 384 numbers per token [`config/train_shakespeare_char.py:21-25`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_shakespeare_char.py#L21-L25).

Two facts frame the rest. It is MIT licensed, copyright Andrej Karpathy [`LICENSE:3`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/LICENSE#L3). And it is retired: since November 2025 the README sends people to its successor, nanochat, and keeps this repo up "for posterity" [`README.md:9`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L9). For a learner that is an advantage: the code you read here will not move under you.

### The one idea: predict the next token

*core · 5 min*

**In short:** Everything in nanoGPT serves one task: given some tokens, predict the token that follows. The data supplies the answers for free, because the right answer is simply the next number in the file.

By the end of this stop you can say what the model is trained to do, and why no labelling is needed.

Take the text `To be or`. Turn each character into a number, a **token id**. Now, at every position, ask: what comes next? After `T` the answer is `o`; after `To` it is a space; after `To ` it is `b`. One sentence gives you as many training examples as it has characters.

`train.py` builds exactly that, in one function. It picks random starting points in the token file, cuts out windows of `block_size` tokens as the input `x`, and cuts the same windows **shifted one position to the right** as the targets `y` [`train.py:123-125`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L123-L125). Position 5 of `y` is the token that follows position 5 of `x`.

The model looks at `x` and outputs, for every position, a score for every possible next token. The **loss** measures how little probability it gave to the real answer from `y`, averaged over all positions [`model.py:184-187`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L184-L187). Training nudges the weights to lower that loss, thousands of times.

Generating text is the same model in a loop: predict a next token, append it, predict again [`model.py:312-328`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L312-L328).

How to read the loss numbers in this guide: with 65 possible characters, a model that guesses uniformly scores ln 65 ≈ 4.17. The README's baby GPT reaches 1.4697 on held-out text [`README.md:51`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L51). Roughly, it gives the right next character a probability of e^−1.47 ≈ 0.23 (a geometric mean over positions), out of 65 options.

> **Checkpoint:** In a training batch, `x[0]` holds the ids for the text `hello`. What does `y[0]` hold?
> - The ids for `hello` again
> - The ids for `ello` followed by whatever character came next in the file
> - A single id: the character after `hello`
> - The ids for `olleh`
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>The ids for `ello` followed by whatever character came next in the file. `y` is cut from the same file starting one position later [`train.py:124-125`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L124-L125), so it is `x` shifted left by one, with one new token at the end.</details>

## Run it

### Run it: train and sample a Shakespeare model

*core · 5 min*

**In short:** Three commands give you a working GPT: prepare the data, train with the Shakespeare config, sample. On a GPU it takes minutes; on a laptop add a few flags and shrink the model.

By the end of this stop you have trained a model and watched it write.

1. **Install**: `pip install torch numpy transformers datasets tiktoken wandb tqdm` [`README.md:22`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L22).
2. **Prepare**: `python data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py` downloads 1 MB of Shakespeare and writes `train.bin`, `val.bin` and `meta.pkl` into `data/shakespeare_char/`.
3. **Train**: `python train.py config/train_shakespeare_char.py`. The config file replaces `train.py`'s GPT-2-sized defaults with a 6-layer model, a 256-character context and 5,000 iterations [`config/train_shakespeare_char.py:16-29`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_shakespeare_char.py#L16-L29). On an A100 the README reports about 3 minutes.
4. **Sample**: `python sample.py --out_dir=out-shakespeare-char`.

**No NVIDIA GPU?** The defaults assume CUDA and `torch.compile` [`train.py:72-74`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L72-L74), so say otherwise. The README's laptop recipe adds `--device=cpu --compile=False` and shrinks everything: context 64, batch 12, 4 layers of 128 channels, 2,000 iterations [`README.md:85`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L85). It also runs in about 3 minutes and reaches a loss near 1.88. On Apple Silicon use `--device=mps`. On Windows keep `--compile=False` [`README.md:224`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L224). Pass the same `--device` to `sample.py`.

**What you should see.** Start-up prints the parameter count, `number of parameters: 10.65M` for the GPU config [`model.py:147-148`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L147-L148). Then come `iter` lines with loss and milliseconds, and every 250 iterations a `step` line with train and val loss. The first val loss sits a little above 4.17. Once it nears 1.5, samples look like a play script: speaker names in capitals, line breaks, invented but plausible words.

### Changing settings: config files and --key=value

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** Every setting is a global variable at the top of the script. A config file is a Python file of assignments that runs over those globals; a `--key=value` flag then overrides one of them, with a strict type check.

By the end you can change any setting without editing code, and you know the two ways it fails.

Open `train.py`: lines 33–74 are plain assignments such as `batch_size = 12` and `learning_rate = 6e-4` [`train.py:47-60`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L47-L60). Line 76 records the name of every global whose value is an int, float, bool or string. Line 77 runs `configurator.py`. Line 78 snapshots the final values into `config`, which is logged and saved in checkpoints [`train.py:76-78`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L76-L78).

`configurator.py` is not imported; its text is executed inside `train.py`'s namespace. It walks the command-line arguments:

- An argument without `=` is a config file, executed as Python [`configurator.py:21-28`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/configurator.py#L21-L28). Later assignments win.
- `--key=value` must name an existing global, or you get `ValueError: Unknown config key` [`configurator.py:46-47`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/configurator.py#L46-L47). The value goes through `literal_eval`, so `True`, `3e-4` and `64` become a bool, a float and an int; anything else stays a string [`configurator.py:34-40`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/configurator.py#L34-L40).
- The new value must have exactly the type of the default [`configurator.py:41-42`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/configurator.py#L41-L42).

So `python train.py config/train_shakespeare_char.py --batch_size=32 --device=cpu` applies the file, then the two flags, in that order. `sample.py` and `bench.py` use the same snippet on their own globals [`sample.py:23`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L23).

Two traps. `--learning_rate=1` is an int and trips the type check; write `1.0`. And because `configurator.py` is opened by a relative path, every script must be run from the repo root.

<details><summary>Go deeper</summary>

Why it is built like this: Karpathy wanted no `config.` prefix on every variable and no configuration framework [`configurator.py:12-14`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/configurator.py#L12-L14). The cost shows in tooling. Your editor cannot tell that a config file changed `n_layer`; there is no `--help`; and a typo inside a config file (say `n_layers = 8`) silently creates a new, unused global instead of raising, because config files are executed, not checked. Only command-line flags get the unknown-key and type checks.

</details>

> **Checkpoint:** You run `python train.py --dropout=0`. What happens?
> - dropout becomes 0.0
> - An AssertionError: `0` parses as an int and the default `0.0` is a float
> - ValueError: Unknown config key
> - The flag is silently ignored
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>An AssertionError: `0` parses as an int and the default `0.0` is a float. `literal_eval('0')` returns the int 0, and the configurator requires the type of the default `dropout = 0.0` [`train.py:55`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L55) to match exactly [`configurator.py:42`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/configurator.py#L42). Write `--dropout=0.0`.</details>

### Run it at scale: OpenWebText, 8 GPUs, baselines, finetuning

*deep · 6 min*

**In short:** Reproducing GPT-2 (124M) is one data command and one torchrun command on an 8×A100 node, about 4 days. The same train.py also evaluates OpenAI's checkpoints and finetunes them.

By the end you know the commands for the big runs and what each one needs.

**Data.** `python data/openwebtext/prepare.py` downloads OpenWebText through Hugging Face `datasets` and writes about 9 billion GPT-2 tokens into a 17 GB `train.bin` [`data/openwebtext/prepare.py:76-78`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/openwebtext/prepare.py#L76-L78). The download itself takes about 54 GB of cache.

**Pretraining.** `torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 train.py config/train_gpt2.py` [`config/train_gpt2.py:1-3`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_gpt2.py#L1-L3). `torchrun` starts 8 processes, one per GPU. Each optimizer step covers 12 × 1024 × 40 = 491,520 tokens across them, for 600,000 steps, 300B tokens in total [`config/train_gpt2.py:9-17`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_gpt2.py#L9-L17). The README reports about 4 days to a loss of about 2.85 [`README.md:121`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L121). Across two machines you run `torchrun` on each with `--nnodes=2`, a `--node_rank` and the master's address [`train.py:11-16`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L11-L16).

**Baselines.** `python train.py config/eval_gpt2.py` loads OpenAI's GPT-2 124M, evaluates once and exits, because the config sets `eval_only = True` [`config/eval_gpt2.py:4-8`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/eval_gpt2.py#L4-L8). OpenAI's model scores about 3.11 on OpenWebText [`README.md:121`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L121). The README attributes the gap to 2.85 to the data: GPT-2 was trained on WebText, which was never released, and OpenWebText is only a reproduction of it [`README.md:156`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L156).

**Finetuning.** `python data/shakespeare/prepare.py`, then `python train.py config/finetune_shakespeare.py`, starts from GPT-2 XL and trains 20 short iterations at a constant 3e-5 [`config/finetune_shakespeare.py:10-25`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/finetune_shakespeare.py#L10-L25). Sample with `python sample.py --out_dir=out-shakespeare`.

**Straight from OpenAI.** `python sample.py --init_from=gpt2-xl --start="..."` generates from the 1.5B-parameter model with no training at all [`README.md:196-201`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L196-L201).

## The stack

### PyTorch in eight minutes, using nanoGPT's own lines

*standard · 8 min*

**In short:** Four PyTorch ideas carry the whole repo: tensors, modules with a `forward` method, autograd's `backward`, and an optimizer step. Each appears in a handful of lines you can point at.

By the end you can read `model.py` and `train.py` without tripping over PyTorch itself.

**Tensors.** A tensor is an array of numbers with a shape, living on the CPU or a GPU. nanoGPT's batches are integer tensors of shape `(batch_size, block_size)`, moved to the device with `.to(device)` [`train.py:126-130`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L126-L130). Inside the model, activations are float tensors of shape `(B, T, C)`: batch, time (position in the sequence) and channels [`model.py:53`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L53).

**Modules.** A layer is a class that subclasses `nn.Module`, creates its weights in `__init__` and computes in `forward`. `MLP` is the cleanest example: two `nn.Linear` layers with a GELU between [`model.py:78-92`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L78-L92). Calling `module(x)` runs `forward`. Modules nest: a `Block` holds an attention module and an `MLP`, and `GPT` holds a list of `Block`s [`model.py:126-132`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L126-L132). `model.parameters()` then finds every weight in the tree.

**Autograd.** PyTorch records how each tensor was computed. `loss.backward()` walks that record backwards and stores in each weight's `.grad` how the loss would change if the weight grew a little. In `train.py` it is `scaler.scale(loss).backward()` [`train.py:304-305`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L304-L305); the scaler only matters for 16-bit training.

**Optimizer.** `optimizer.step()` moves every weight a small amount against its gradient, and `zero_grad` clears the gradients for the next round [`train.py:310-314`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L310-L314). nanoGPT uses AdamW, built in `GPT.configure_optimizers`.

Two switches you will meet: `model.eval()` and `model.train()` turn dropout off and on [`train.py:218-227`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L218-L227), and `@torch.no_grad()` skips the autograd record when you only need outputs [`train.py:215-216`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L215-L216).

### Tokens and tokenizers: characters versus GPT-2's BPE

*standard · 6 min*

**In short:** A tokenizer turns text into integer ids and back. nanoGPT uses two: one id per character (65 ids for Shakespeare) and GPT-2's byte-pair encoding (50,257 ids, through tiktoken).

By the end you can say what a token is in each dataset and why it sets the model's vocabulary size.

**Character level.** `data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py` collects every distinct character in the text, sorts them and numbers them [`data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py:23-31`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py#L23-L31). The result is 65 tokens: newline, space, punctuation, one digit and both cases of the alphabet [`data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py:63-68`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py#L63-L68). `encode` maps each character through `stoi`; `decode` maps back through `itos`. Simple, but the model must spell every word letter by letter, so a 500-token sample is only 500 characters.

**Byte-pair encoding (BPE).** GPT-2's tokenizer starts from bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent neighbouring pair into a new token, until it has 50,257 of them. Common words become one token; rare words become several. nanoGPT uses OpenAI's `tiktoken` library for it [`data/shakespeare/prepare.py:19-22`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare/prepare.py#L19-L22). The same 1,115,394 characters of Shakespeare become 301,966 + 36,059 BPE tokens instead of 1,003,854 + 111,540 characters [`data/shakespeare/prepare.py:32-33`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare/prepare.py#L32-L33): about 3.3 characters per token.

**Why uint16.** Both vocabularies have fewer than 65,536 ids, so every id fits in 2 bytes; GPT-2's largest is 50,256 [`data/openwebtext/prepare.py:62`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/openwebtext/prepare.py#L62). That halves the 9-billion-token OpenWebText file compared with 32-bit integers.

**End of text.** OpenWebText appends GPT-2's special `<|endoftext|>` token (id 50256) after every document, so the model sees where documents end [`data/openwebtext/prepare.py:43-46`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/openwebtext/prepare.py#L43-L46).

The vocabulary size flows straight into the model: it is the number of rows in the embedding table and the width of the output layer [`model.py:127-133`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L127-L133).

> **Checkpoint:** Why can nanoGPT store token ids as uint16?
> - PyTorch requires 16-bit inputs
> - Every id in both vocabularies is below 65,536, the largest uint16
> - uint16 compresses the text
> - The model trains in 16-bit precision
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>Every id in both vocabularies is below 65,536, the largest uint16. The comment says it outright: GPT-2's largest id is 50,256, below 2^16 [`data/openwebtext/prepare.py:62`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/openwebtext/prepare.py#L62). The ids are converted to int64 only when a batch is built.</details>

### Mixed precision: bfloat16, float16 and the GradScaler

*standard · 6 min*

**In short:** Most of the arithmetic runs in 16-bit floats, which GPUs do much faster, while the weights stay 32-bit. bfloat16 needs nothing else; float16 needs a GradScaler so small gradients do not round to zero.

By the end you know what `dtype`, `ctx` and `scaler` do in `train.py`.

A normal float has 32 bits. GPUs do 16-bit matrix maths far faster: an A100 is rated at 312 TFLOPS in bfloat16, the figure `estimate_mfu` uses [`model.py:301`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L301), against 19.5 TFLOPS in plain float32. 16-bit tensors also take half the memory. There are two 16-bit formats. **float16** keeps more precision but has a small range: values below about 6e-8 become zero. **bfloat16** keeps float32's range with less precision. `train.py` picks bfloat16 when the GPU supports it, otherwise float16 [`train.py:73`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L73).

**Autocast.** You do not convert the model yourself. `torch.amp.autocast` is a context in which PyTorch runs each operation in 16-bit where that is safe (matrix multiplies) and in 32-bit where it is not (softmax, sums). On CPU nanoGPT uses an empty context instead [`train.py:109-112`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L109-L112). Every forward pass sits inside `with ctx:` [`train.py:299-300`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L299-L300).

**GradScaler.** In float16, many gradients are smaller than the format can hold. The scaler multiplies the loss by a large factor before `backward`, so the gradients are big enough to survive, and divides them back before the update. It has to unscale before clipping, or the clip threshold would apply to inflated numbers [`train.py:306-312`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L306-L312). If the scaled gradients overflow, `scaler.step` skips that update and lowers the factor. For bfloat16 and float32 the scaler is created disabled, and every call on it does nothing [`train.py:195-196`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L195-L196).

**TF32.** Two more lines allow TensorFloat-32, a mode on NVIDIA Ampere and newer GPUs that runs float32 matrix multiplies faster with slightly fewer mantissa bits [`train.py:107-108`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L107-L108).

> **Checkpoint:** You train on a GPU without bfloat16 support. Which line keeps tiny gradients from rounding to zero?
> - `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True`
> - `scaler.scale(loss).backward()`
> - `model.eval()`
> - `torch.manual_seed(1337 + seed_offset)`
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>`scaler.scale(loss).backward()`. Without bf16, `dtype` falls back to float16, which enables the GradScaler [`train.py:196`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L196); scaling the loss before `backward` scales every gradient up with it [`train.py:305`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L305).</details>

### Many GPUs: torchrun, DDP and gradient accumulation

*standard · 6 min*

**In short:** Gradient accumulation fakes a big batch on one GPU by adding up gradients over several small ones. DDP runs one process per GPU and averages their gradients. nanoGPT combines the two so 1 GPU and 8 GPUs take the same 491,520-token step.

By the end you can explain what changes when you launch with `torchrun`.

**The big-batch problem.** GPT-2-style training wants about half a million tokens per optimizer step, far more than fits in one GPU's memory at once. The default micro-batch is 12 sequences of 1,024 tokens, tuned in commit `9f95aca` "for gpt2 124M model on A100 40GB". So `train.py` runs `gradient_accumulation_steps` forward/backward passes before each update, and the gradients add up in `.grad` between them [`train.py:290-305`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L290-L305). Each loss is divided by the number of micro-steps, so the sum is an average [`train.py:301`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L301). The default is 5 × 8 = 40 micro-steps [`train.py:48`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L48).

**DDP.** `torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py` starts 8 copies of the script and gives each the environment variables `RANK`, `LOCAL_RANK` and `WORLD_SIZE`. `train.py` sees `RANK`, joins the process group and claims GPU number `LOCAL_RANK` [`train.py:82-91`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L82-L91). Each process gets its own random seed, so each draws different batches [`train.py:106`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L106). The model is wrapped in `DDP` [`train.py:210-212`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L210-L212), which averages gradients across processes during `backward`, so all 8 copies take the identical step.

**Together.** With 8 processes, each runs 40 / 8 = 5 micro-steps [`train.py:92-95`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L92-L95), and tokens per step stay at 5 × 8 × 12 × 1,024 = 491,520 [`train.py:101-102`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L101-L102). Averaging across GPUs after every micro-step would waste bandwidth, so the sync is switched on only for the last one [`train.py:298`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L298).

**One boss.** Only rank 0, the `master_process`, evaluates, prints and saves checkpoints [`train.py:263`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L263).

> **Checkpoint:** You launch on 4 GPUs with the default settings. How many micro-steps does each process run per iteration, and how many tokens does one optimizer step see?
> - 40 each; 4 × 491,520 tokens
> - 10 each; 491,520 tokens
> - 5 each; 245,760 tokens
> - 1 each; 49,152 tokens
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>10 each; 491,520 tokens. 40 is divided by the world size of 4 [`train.py:95`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L95), and tokens per step are 10 × 4 × 12 × 1,024 = 491,520, the same as on 8 GPUs or 1.</details>

## The map

### The map: three scripts that pass files along

*core · 4 min*

**In short:** Data scripts write token files; `train.py` turns them into `ckpt.pt` using the GPT from `model.py`; `sample.py` turns `ckpt.pt` back into text. Files on disk are the only interface between the stages.

By the end you can place every file in the repo on the pipeline.

Picture an assembly line with three stations and a box passed between them.

1. **Prepare** (`data/<name>/prepare.py`): raw text in, `train.bin` and `val.bin` out, each the whole corpus as one long row of 16-bit integers. The character dataset also writes `meta.pkl`, its vocabulary.
2. **Train** (`train.py`): reads `data/<dataset>/train.bin` [`train.py:114-120`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L114-L120), builds a `GPT` from `model.py` [`train.py:30`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L30), trains it and writes `out_dir/ckpt.pt` [`train.py:285-286`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L285-L286).
3. **Sample** (`sample.py`): reads `out_dir/ckpt.pt` [`sample.py:35-38`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L35-L38), rebuilds the same `GPT` and prints generated text.

Two side doors. `train.py` and `sample.py` can start from OpenAI's GPT-2 weights instead (`init_from='gpt2'` and its larger siblings). And `bench.py` uses `model.py` alone to time training steps.

What is *not* here matters as much: no package to install, no command-line parser, no server, no classes outside `model.py`. Each script runs top to bottom as plain Python, configured by global variables that `configurator.py` overwrites. `model.py` is the only file other files import, so it is the one place where a change reaches everything.

Where the assembly-line picture stops working: the box is not generic. A checkpoint belongs to its dataset. `sample.py` decodes with the vocabulary of the dataset named inside the checkpoint, so a character model and a GPT-2-token model are not interchangeable.

> **Checkpoint:** You change the MLP's width in `model.py`. Which scripts are affected?
> - Only train.py
> - train.py, sample.py and bench.py, because all three import model.py
> - Only the prepare scripts
> - None until you rerun prepare.py
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>train.py, sample.py and bench.py, because all three import model.py. All three scripts start with the same import [`train.py:30`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L30) [`sample.py:9`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L9) [`bench.py:9`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/bench.py#L9). Old checkpoints also stop loading, because the weight shapes no longer match.</details>

### Inside class GPT: the module tree and where the parameters live

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** A GPT is an embedding table, a stack of identical blocks, a final LayerNorm and an output layer that shares the embedding's weights. Nearly all parameters sit in the blocks and the token embedding.

By the end you can sketch the model and estimate its size on paper.

`GPT.__init__` builds one `ModuleDict` called `transformer`, plus `lm_head` [`model.py:126-133`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L126-L133):

- `wte`: the token embedding, `vocab_size` × `n_embd`.
- `wpe`: the position embedding, `block_size` × `n_embd`.
- `drop`: dropout on their sum.
- `h`: a list of `n_layer` `Block`s.
- `ln_f`: a final LayerNorm.
- `lm_head`: a linear layer from `n_embd` to `vocab_size`, without bias, whose weight *is* `wte`'s weight [`model.py:138`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L138).

Every shape comes from `GPTConfig`, seven fields whose defaults describe GPT-2 small [`model.py:108-116`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L108-L116).

**Where the parameters are.** Each block holds about 12 × n_embd² weights: the query/key/value projection is n_embd × 3·n_embd, attention's output projection n_embd × n_embd, and the MLP's two layers n_embd × 4·n_embd each. For the baby GPT that is 12 × 384² ≈ 1.77M per block, and 6 blocks make about 10.6M. The 65-row token embedding adds only 25K. Hence `number of parameters: 10.65M` at start-up. For GPT-2 small, 12 blocks × 12 × 768² ≈ 85M, and the 50,257 × 768 token embedding adds 38.6M, for about 124M in all.

The printed count leaves out `wpe` but keeps `wte`, because the tied matrix also serves as the output layer [`model.py:150-160`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L150-L160).

**Initialisation.** `_init_weights` draws every linear and embedding weight from a normal distribution with standard deviation 0.02 [`model.py:162-168`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L162-L168). The concepts chapter explains the one exception.

## Core ideas

### Embeddings: turning ids into vectors

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** Each token id picks a row from a learned table, and each position picks a row from a second table. Their sum is the vector that enters the first block.

By the end you know exactly what the model sees at its input.

An integer like 46 says nothing about meaning; 46 is not "close" to 47 in any useful way. So the model keeps a table, `wte`, with one row of `n_embd` learned numbers per token id. Looking up row 46 gives a vector of 384 numbers in the baby GPT, 768 in GPT-2 [`model.py:127`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L127). Training moves the rows until tokens that behave alike get similar vectors.

Attention, as the next lessons show, treats its inputs as an unordered set. To tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog" the model must know where each token sits. nanoGPT uses the simplest fix: a second table, `wpe`, with one learned row per position up to `block_size` [`model.py:128`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L128). In `forward`, positions are just `0..t-1`; both lookups happen and the vectors are added [`model.py:174-179`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L174-L179). Shapes: `(b, t, n_embd)` plus `(t, n_embd)` broadcasts to `(b, t, n_embd)`.

Two consequences follow.

- The model cannot read more than `block_size` tokens, because there is no row for position 256 in the baby GPT. `forward` asserts it [`model.py:173`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L173), and `generate` crops its input to the last `block_size` tokens [`model.py:313-314`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L313-L314).
- `crop_block_size` can shorten a trained model's context by slicing `wpe` [`model.py:195-201`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L195-L201), but nothing in the repo can lengthen it.

The same `wte` matrix is reused at the very end to score the next token (weight tying), so a token's input vector and its output score are tied together.

### The transformer block: attention, MLP, two residual adds

*core · 5 min*

**In short:** A block refines every position's vector in two steps: attention mixes in information from earlier positions, then a small MLP processes each position on its own. Each step's output is added to its input rather than replacing it.

By the end you can explain the two lines of `Block.forward`.

```python
x = x + self.attn(self.ln_1(x))
x = x + self.mlp(self.ln_2(x))
```

That is the whole block [`model.py:103-106`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L103-L106). Read it as a meeting followed by desk work.

1. **LayerNorm** rescales each position's vector to mean 0 and variance 1, then applies a learned gain [`model.py:26-27`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L26-L27). It keeps the numbers in a steady range however deep the stack gets.
2. **Attention** is the meeting: each position looks back at earlier positions and pulls in what is relevant. It is the only place where positions exchange information. The next lesson takes it apart.
3. **The MLP** is the desk work: each position, alone, goes through a two-layer network that widens to 4 × `n_embd` (1,536 in the baby GPT), applies GELU, and narrows back [`model.py:80-92`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L80-L92). GELU is a smooth version of "keep positives, zero out negatives".
4. **Residual adds.** Each sub-layer's output is *added* to `x`. Think of `x` as a shared notebook that every block writes notes into rather than rewriting. Gradients flow straight back through the additions, which is what lets 12 or 48 blocks train at all.

Where the analogy stops: in a real meeting people speak in turn. Here every position attends at the same moment, and all of it is one batch of matrix maths.

Normalising *before* each sub-layer ("pre-norm") is GPT-2's arrangement; the original 2017 transformer normalised after. Because of pre-norm, the stack needs one last LayerNorm, `ln_f`, before the output layer [`model.py:182`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L182).

A GPT is this block repeated: 6 times in the baby GPT, 12 in GPT-2 small, 48 in GPT-2 XL [`model.py:216-221`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L216-L221). Every copy has the same shape and its own weights.

> **Checkpoint:** Which part of a block is the only place where one position can use information from another?
> - LayerNorm
> - The MLP
> - Attention
> - The residual add
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>Attention. LayerNorm and the MLP act on each position separately. Only attention multiplies across the time dimension, producing a T × T table per head [`model.py:61`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L61).</details>

### Causal self-attention, line by line

*core · 7 min*

**In short:** Each position asks a question (query); every earlier position offers a label (key) and some content (value). The position takes an average of the values, weighted by how well each key matches its query. Heads let it ask several questions at once.

By the end you can follow `CausalSelfAttention.forward` and say what each shape means.

Analogy: a library search. Your **query** is what you are looking for; each book has a **key** (its catalogue entry) and a **value** (its contents). You score every key against your query, turn the scores into weights that sum to 1, and read a blend of the contents. Where it breaks: here you are also a book, and you may only search books shelved before you.

**1. Project.** One linear layer turns each position's vector into query, key and value at once, `3 × n_embd` numbers, then splits them [`model.py:56`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L56).

**2. Split into heads.** Each of q, k, v is reshaped from `(B, T, C)` to `(B, n_head, T, C / n_head)` [`model.py:57-59`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L57-L59). The baby GPT has 6 heads of 64 numbers; each head searches independently.

**3. Score.** Every query is compared with every key by dot product, scaled by 1/√64, giving a `(T, T)` table per head [`model.py:67`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L67).

**4. Mask the future.** Entries where the key comes after the query are set to −∞, using a lower-triangular matrix [`model.py:68`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L68). This is what "causal" means: position 5 cannot peek at token 6, the one it is meant to predict.

**5. Weights.** Softmax turns each row into weights that sum to 1; −∞ becomes exactly 0 [`model.py:69`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L69).

**6. Blend.** Multiply by the values, so each position gets a weighted average of earlier values [`model.py:71`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L71).

**7. Reassemble.** The heads are laid side by side again and mixed by one more linear layer, `c_proj` [`model.py:72-75`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L72-L75).

On PyTorch 2.0 and later, steps 3 to 6 run as one fused call with `is_causal=True` [`model.py:62-64`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L62-L64). It computes the same result without storing the T × T table, which is why it is faster. The manual path stays in the file as the readable version.

<details><summary>Go deeper</summary>

**Why divide by √(head size)?** For random vectors of length d, a dot product has variance about d. Dividing by √d keeps scores near unit scale, so the softmax does not collapse into picking a single key at initialisation.

**Dropout.** In the manual path, dropout is applied to the attention weights [`model.py:70`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L70). In the fused path it is passed as `dropout_p`, and only while training [`model.py:64`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L64). A late fix (`7399dfe`, "dont always dropout!") added the `if self.training` part, so evaluation and sampling of models trained with dropout used to be noisier than intended.

**The mask buffer.** The lower-triangular matrix is registered as a buffer named `bias` only when Flash attention is missing [`model.py:46-50`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L46-L50). That name collides with the idea of a bias parameter, which is why `from_pretrained` filters keys ending in `.attn.bias`.

</details>

> **Checkpoint:** You delete the `masked_fill` line from the manual attention path and train. What goes wrong?
> - Nothing; softmax already ignores the future
> - Training loss falls far lower than normal, but generation is poor, because each position could see the very token it was asked to predict
> - A shape error on the first batch
> - Attention becomes slower
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>Training loss falls far lower than normal, but generation is poor, because each position could see the very token it was asked to predict. The mask is the only thing hiding later positions [`model.py:68`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L68). Without it, predicting `y[t] = x[t+1]` becomes copying, which works in training (where x[t+1] is present) and fails in sampling (where it is not yet written).</details>

### AdamW and weight decay, as nanoGPT sets them up

*standard · 6 min*

**In short:** AdamW moves each weight against a smoothed version of its gradient, with a step size adapted to that weight, and shrinks weights slightly every step. nanoGPT applies that shrinking (weight decay 0.1) only to matrices, never to biases or LayerNorm gains.

By the end you can read `configure_optimizers` and the `beta1`, `beta2` and `weight_decay` settings.

Plain gradient descent subtracts `learning_rate × gradient` from each weight. **Adam** keeps two running averages per weight: the average gradient (momentum, controlled by `beta1 = 0.9`) and the average squared gradient (controlled by `beta2 = 0.95`) [`train.py:57-62`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L57-L62). The step is the first divided by the square root of the second. A weight with consistently large gradients takes a normal-sized step, not a huge one; a weight with tiny, noisy gradients still moves. The cost is memory: two extra numbers per weight, which is why the notebook estimates a GPT-2 124M checkpoint with optimizer state at 3 × the weights' size [`transformer_sizing.ipynb:134-139`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/transformer_sizing.ipynb#L134-L139).

The **W** is decoupled weight decay: each step also shrinks every decayed weight towards zero by `learning_rate × weight_decay × weight`, which discourages any one weight from growing large.

nanoGPT's rule for what to decay is two list comprehensions: every tensor with 2 or more dimensions (linear-layer weights and the embedding) is decayed; every 1-D tensor (biases, LayerNorm gains) is not [`model.py:268-275`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L268-L275). For the baby GPT, start-up prints 26 decayed tensors with 10,740,096 numbers and 13 non-decayed tensors with 4,992 [`model.py:276-279`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L276-L279).

On CUDA it asks for the **fused** AdamW kernel when PyTorch offers one, which updates all tensors in a single GPU call [`model.py:280-285`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L280-L285).

The baby config raises `beta2` to 0.99 because each iteration sees few tokens [`config/train_shakespeare_char.py:31`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_shakespeare_char.py#L31). At 64 × 256 = 16,384 tokens per step the gradients are noisy, and a longer average of their squares is steadier.

> **Checkpoint:** Which of these parameters gets weight decay in nanoGPT?
> - `transformer.ln_f.weight`, a LayerNorm gain
> - `h.0.attn.c_proj.bias`
> - `transformer.wte.weight`, the token embedding
> - None; weight_decay only lowers the learning rate
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>`transformer.wte.weight`, the token embedding. The rule is purely by shape: 2-D tensors are decayed [`model.py:270`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L270). The embedding is a 2-D matrix; gains and biases are 1-D.</details>

### The learning-rate schedule: warmup, then cosine

*standard · 4 min*

**In short:** The learning rate climbs linearly from almost zero to its maximum over `warmup_iters` steps, follows half a cosine wave down to `min_lr` by `lr_decay_iters`, and then stays there.

By the end you can predict the learning rate at any iteration.

`get_lr(it)` has three cases [`train.py:230-242`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L230-L242):

1. **Warmup**, while `it < warmup_iters`: `learning_rate × (it + 1) / (warmup_iters + 1)`. At the start the weights are random and the gradients point in wild directions; small steps keep AdamW's running averages from being dominated by that noise. The `+ 1` makes the very first step non-zero, a fix from December 2024 (`dc81cb3`).
2. **After the schedule**, once `it > lr_decay_iters`: `min_lr`.
3. **In between**: `coeff = 0.5 × (1 + cos(π × progress))` runs smoothly from 1 to 0, and the rate is `min_lr + coeff × (learning_rate − min_lr)`.

The loop writes the value into the optimizer at the top of each iteration, unless `decay_lr = False`, in which case it stays at `learning_rate` [`train.py:257-260`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L257-L260).

Concrete numbers. GPT-2 defaults: 2,000 warmup steps to 6e-4, then cosine down to 6e-5 at step 600,000. The comments cite Chinchilla for `lr_decay_iters ≈ max_iters` and `min_lr ≈ learning_rate / 10` [`train.py:64-68`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L64-L68). Baby GPT: 100 warmup steps to 1e-3, down to 1e-4 at step 5,000 [`config/train_shakespeare_char.py:27-33`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_shakespeare_char.py#L27-L33). Finetuning: a constant 3e-5, because the weights already work and large steps would undo them [`config/finetune_shakespeare.py:23-25`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/finetune_shakespeare.py#L23-L25).

A common mistake is shortening `max_iters` without shortening `lr_decay_iters`. The run then stops while the rate is still high, before the low-rate phase. The README's CPU recipe sets both to 2,000 for that reason [`README.md:88`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/README.md#L88).

> **Checkpoint:** With the baby config, what is the learning rate at iteration 50?
> - 1e-3
> - About 5e-4
> - 1e-4
> - 0
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>About 5e-4. Iteration 50 is inside the 100-step warmup, so it is 1e-3 × 51 / 101 ≈ 5.05e-4 [`train.py:233-234`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L233-L234).</details>

### Sampling: how the model writes, one token at a time

*core · 4 min*

**In short:** `generate` repeats one step: run the model on the text so far, take the scores for the next token, sharpen or flatten them with temperature, keep the top k, draw one token at random, append it.

By the end you can explain what `--temperature` and `--top_k` do and why two samples differ.

`GPT.generate` is a loop of `max_new_tokens` steps [`model.py:305-330`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L305-L330):

1. **Crop** the running sequence to its last `block_size` tokens; the model cannot see further back [`model.py:313-314`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L313-L314).
2. **Score** with one forward pass. Without targets, `forward` computes logits for the last position only, the only ones needed [`model.py:188-191`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L188-L191).
3. **Temperature**: divide the logits by `temperature` [`model.py:318`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L318). Below 1 the gaps between scores widen and the favourite wins more often; above 1 they shrink and unlikely tokens get a chance. `sample.py` uses 0.8 [`sample.py:17`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L17).
4. **Top-k**: every score below the k-th highest becomes −∞, so only k tokens can be drawn [`model.py:320-322`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L320-L322). `sample.py` uses k = 200.
5. **Draw**: softmax turns scores into probabilities and `torch.multinomial` picks one token at random in proportion [`model.py:324-326`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L324-L326).
6. **Append** and repeat.

Step 5's randomness is why the 10 default samples differ from each other; the fixed seed of 1337 is why rerunning `sample.py` reproduces the same 10 [`sample.py:19-27`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L19-L27).

Each step reruns the whole model on up to `block_size` tokens, recomputing everything for the earlier positions. Production systems cache those intermediate results (a "KV cache"); nanoGPT does not, which keeps `generate` to a dozen lines and makes long generations slower.

For the 65-character model, `top_k = 200` exceeds the vocabulary, so `min(top_k, vocab)` keeps all 65 [`model.py:321`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L321), a fix from `91d0251`.

> **Checkpoint:** You run `sample.py` twice with the same flags and get identical text. Why?
> - top_k removes the randomness
> - The seed is fixed at 1337, so the random draws repeat
> - Temperature 0.8 is deterministic
> - The model caches its outputs between runs
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>The seed is fixed at 1337, so the random draws repeat. `sample.py` seeds PyTorch's random generator before sampling [`sample.py:26-27`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L26-L27), so `torch.multinomial` makes the same draws. Pass `--seed=` with another number for different text.</details>

### Initialisation: where the weights start

*deep · 4 min*

**In short:** All weights start as small random numbers (standard deviation 0.02), and the two projections in each block that write into the residual stream start even smaller, scaled by 1/√(2 × n_layer). A fresh model's loss should therefore be close to ln(vocab_size).

By the end you can say what a fresh model's loss should be and what the special initialisation is for.

`GPT.__init__` calls `self.apply(self._init_weights)`, which visits every module. Linear layers get weights from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.02, and zero biases; embeddings get the same normal distribution [`model.py:162-168`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L162-L168). Small weights give small logits, so the first softmax is nearly uniform and the first loss is close to ln(65) ≈ 4.17 for characters, or ln(50,304) ≈ 10.8 for GPT-2's vocabulary. If your first evaluation prints much more than that, look here first.

Then a second pass finds every parameter named `c_proj.weight`, the output projections of attention and of the MLP, and re-draws it with standard deviation 0.02 / √(2 × n_layer) [`model.py:142-145`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L142-L145). For the baby GPT that is 0.02 / √12 ≈ 0.0058. Each block adds two outputs into the residual stream, so a 6-layer model sums 12 of them; shrinking each one keeps their total from growing with depth. The comment credits the GPT-2 paper, and Karpathy's commit reports the effect was large: "it makes a ton of difference and works much better than default" (`f29a9ff`).

The weight tie used to matter here. `wte.weight` is set to `lm_head`'s tensor [`model.py:133-138`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L133-L138), and commit `43b37fd` chose that direction so that "the final layer init is preserved". At the time, PyTorch's default embedding initialisation (standard deviation 1) would otherwise have ended up in the output layer. Today `_init_weights` gives both modules the same 0.02, so the direction no longer changes anything. That last point is inferred from the dates: `43b37fd` is from 14 January 2023, the custom initialisation `f29a9ff` from 27 January.

## How it flows

### Follow the data: from Shakespeare's text to generated text

*core · 6 min*

**In short:** Text becomes ids on disk, ids become batches, batches train a GPT that is saved to `ckpt.pt`, and `sample.py` reloads it, encodes a prompt with the same vocabulary and decodes what the model writes.

By the end you can name every function the quick start runs, in order. Step through the flow below for the code; this lesson is the thread that ties the steps together.

**The vocabulary is the thread.** `prepare.py` invents it (65 characters, sorted) and saves it in `meta.pkl` [`data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py:54-61`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py#L54-L61). `train.py` reads only its size, to shape the embedding table and the output layer [`train.py:137-155`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L137-L155). `sample.py` needs the full tables, to turn your prompt into ids and the output back into text. It finds them through the dataset name the checkpoint stored in its `config` [`sample.py:56-60`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L56-L60). If `meta.pkl` is missing, `sample.py` falls back to GPT-2's tokenizer [`sample.py:69-74`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L69-L74); GPT-2 ids run up to 50,256, so they do not fit a 65-row embedding table and the first forward pass fails.

**The checkpoint is the hand-off.** Training writes one dict to `out-shakespeare-char/ckpt.pt` [`train.py:277-286`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L277-L286). Its `model_args` let `sample.py` rebuild the identical architecture before loading the weights [`sample.py:37-46`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L37-L46); without them, the weights would have nowhere to go.

**Two uses of one model.** In training, the model sees 64 windows of 256 characters and returns a loss. In sampling, it sees one growing sequence and returns scores for the last position only. It is the same `forward`, with and without targets [`model.py:184-193`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L184-L193).

**Saving is selective here.** The Shakespeare config turns off `always_save_checkpoint`, because a 1 MB dataset overfits: validation loss bottoms out and climbs while training loss keeps falling, and you want the bottom [`config/train_shakespeare_char.py:9-10`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_shakespeare_char.py#L9-L10).

**Flow: Prepare Shakespeare, train a baby GPT, sample from it** (trigger: You run the README quick start: `python data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py`, then `python train.py config/train_shakespeare_char.py`, then `python sample.py --out_dir=out-shakespeare-char`.)

1. **Download the text once** [`data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py:12-20`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py#L12-L20) If `input.txt` is missing next to the script, it fetches the 1 MB tiny-Shakespeare file from Karpathy's char-rnn repo, then reads it into one string.
2. **Build a 65-character vocabulary** [`data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py:23-35`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py#L23-L35) Every distinct character, sorted, gets an id. `stoi` maps character to id and `itos` maps back.
3. **Split 90/10 and encode** [`data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py:37-46`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py#L37-L46) The first 90% of the text is training data and the last 10% validation, giving 1,003,854 and 111,540 tokens.
4. **Write token files and meta.pkl** [`data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py:48-61`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py#L48-L61) The ids are written as raw `uint16` bytes. The vocabulary goes into `meta.pkl` so later scripts can use it.
5. **train.py applies the config file** [`train.py:76-78`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L76-L78) The defaults at the top of `train.py` are overwritten by `config/train_shakespeare_char.py`, which sets the dataset, a 6-layer model and 5,000 iterations [`config/train_shakespeare_char.py:16-29`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_shakespeare_char.py#L16-L29).
6. **Read vocab_size from meta.pkl** [`train.py:137-144`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L137-L144) Finding `data/shakespeare_char/meta.pkl`, it sets the vocab size to 65 instead of GPT-2's 50304.
7. **Build a fresh GPT** [`train.py:146-157`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L146-L157) `init_from` defaults to `'scratch'`, so it creates a randomly initialised `GPT` with 10.65M parameters.
8. **Loop: batch, forward, backward, step** [`train.py:290-314`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L290-L314) Each iteration samples 64 random 256-character windows, computes the loss, backpropagates and updates the weights. The flow "One training iteration" traces this step by step.
9. **Evaluate every 250 steps and save on improvement** [`train.py:262-286`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L262-L286) The config sets `always_save_checkpoint = False` [`config/train_shakespeare_char.py:9-10`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/config/train_shakespeare_char.py#L9-L10), so `ckpt.pt` is only rewritten when validation loss beats the best so far.
10. **sample.py rebuilds the model from ckpt.pt** [`sample.py:34-46`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L34-L46) The saved `model_args` recreate the same architecture, and the saved weights are loaded into it.
11. **Find meta.pkl through the checkpoint's config** [`sample.py:56-68`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L56-L68) The checkpoint remembers `dataset = 'shakespeare_char'`, so `sample.py` loads that folder's `meta.pkl` and decodes with characters instead of GPT-2 tokens.
12. **Encode the prompt and generate** [`sample.py:76-89`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L76-L89) The default prompt is a single newline. It generates 10 samples of 500 new characters and prints each one decoded.
13. **One token at a time** [`model.py:305-330`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L305-L330) `generate` runs the model, takes the scores for the last position, applies temperature and top-k, draws one id at random, appends it, and repeats.

> **Checkpoint:** You copy `out-shakespeare-char/ckpt.pt` to a machine that has the repo but never ran `prepare.py`. What happens when you sample from it?
> - It works; the checkpoint contains everything
> - `sample.py` finds no `data/shakespeare_char/meta.pkl`, falls back to GPT-2 encodings, and the ids do not fit the 65-token model
> - It retrains the model
> - It downloads Shakespeare again
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>`sample.py` finds no `data/shakespeare_char/meta.pkl`, falls back to GPT-2 encodings, and the ids do not fit the 65-token model. The checkpoint stores the dataset name, not the vocabulary [`sample.py:58-60`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/sample.py#L58-L60). Copy `meta.pkl` along with `ckpt.pt`.</details>

### One forward pass, with the shapes

*core · 6 min*

**In short:** Ids of shape (B, T) become vectors of shape (B, T, C), keep that shape through every block, and leave as scores of shape (B, T, vocab_size). Cross-entropy against the targets turns them into one number, the loss.

By the end you can track the tensor shapes through `GPT.forward` for the baby GPT. Step through the flow below for the code; this lesson keeps the numbers.

The training call is `model(X, Y)` with X and Y of shape `(64, 256)`, integers from 0 to 64 [`train.py:299-300`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L299-L300).

- `idx`, the token ids: 64 × 256
- `tok_emb + pos_emb`: 64 × 256 × 384
- after each of the 6 blocks: still 64 × 256 × 384
- q, k and v inside attention: 64 × 6 × 256 × 64 (batch, head, position, head size)
- attention weights: 64 × 6 × 256 × 256
- the MLP's hidden layer: 64 × 256 × 1,536
- `logits`: 64 × 256 × 65
- `loss`: one number

Three things to notice.

**The width never changes between blocks.** That is what lets you stack any number of them, and what makes the residual adds possible [`model.py:180-182`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L180-L182).

**The attention table grows with T².** At GPT-2 size, T = 1,024 and 12 heads give 12.6M scores per sequence per layer. That is why the fused Flash kernel, which never stores the table, matters.

**The loss flattens everything.** `logits.view(-1, 65)` and `targets.view(-1)` turn 64 × 256 predictions into 16,384 separate classification problems, and `F.cross_entropy` averages them [`model.py:186-187`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L186-L187). Every position in every window is a training example, which is why one batch carries so much signal.

At sampling time the same function runs with `targets=None` and returns logits of shape `(1, 1, 65)`: one sequence, last position only [`model.py:188-191`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L188-L191).

**Flow: One forward pass: from token ids to a loss** (trigger: `train.py` calls `model(X, Y)` with X and Y of shape (batch_size, block_size), e.g. (64, 256) for the Shakespeare config.)

1. **Check the length and make positions** [`model.py:170-174`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L170-L174) A sequence longer than `block_size` is rejected. Positions are simply 0, 1, …, t-1.
2. **Look up token and position embeddings, add them** [`model.py:176-179`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L176-L179) Each id becomes an `n_embd`-long vector (384 numbers in the baby GPT), plus a vector for its position. The result has shape (B, T, n_embd).
3. **Run every block in order** [`model.py:180-181`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L180-L181) 6 blocks for the baby GPT, 12 for GPT-2 small. Each keeps the shape (B, T, n_embd).
4. **Inside a block: attention, then MLP, each added back** [`model.py:103-106`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L103-L106) LayerNorm first, then the sub-layer, then add the result to the input (a residual connection).
5. **Make queries, keys and values for all heads** [`model.py:55-59`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L55-L59) One linear layer produces all three at once (3 × n_embd wide); each is reshaped to (B, n_head, T, head_size).
6. **Causal attention** [`model.py:61-71`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L61-L71) With PyTorch 2.0 the fused kernel does it with `is_causal=True`; otherwise the manual path computes scores, masks the future with -inf, softmaxes and mixes the values.
7. **Merge heads and project** [`model.py:72-76`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L72-L76) The heads are placed side by side again and one more linear layer mixes them.
8. **The MLP** [`model.py:87-92`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L87-L92) Widen to 4 × n_embd, GELU, narrow back, dropout.
9. **Final LayerNorm** [`model.py:182`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L182) One last normalisation before reading out predictions.
10. **Scores for every vocabulary entry, then the loss** [`model.py:184-187`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L184-L187) `lm_head` gives (B, T, vocab_size) logits. Cross-entropy averages over all B × T positions how surprised the model was by the real next token.
11. **When sampling, only the last position** [`model.py:188-193`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L188-L193) Without targets, only the final position's logits are computed, since only that one is used to pick the next token.

> **Checkpoint:** In the baby GPT, what is the shape of `logits` during training?
> - (64, 65)
> - (64, 256, 384)
> - (64, 256, 65)
> - (16384,)
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>(64, 256, 65). `lm_head` maps each of the 64 × 256 positions from 384 channels to 65 scores [`model.py:133`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L133). It is flattened to (16384, 65) only inside the loss call.</details>

### One training iteration, in order

*core · 7 min*

**In short:** An iteration sets the learning rate, sometimes evaluates and saves, runs forward and backward `gradient_accumulation_steps` times, clips the gradient, takes one AdamW step and frees the gradients. Everything else in `train.py` is setup for this loop.

By the end you can explain the order of operations inside `while True:` and why it is that order. Step through the flow below for each line; the order is the lesson.

Three words first. A **micro-step** is one forward and backward pass on one small batch; with **gradient accumulation**, several micro-steps add their gradients together before a single weight update, as if they were one big batch. **Autocast** runs the maths in 16-bit floats where that is safe, for speed. **AdamW** is the optimizer: the rule that turns gradients into weight changes.

1. **Learning rate first** [`train.py:257-260`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L257-L260), so the step about to happen uses this iteration's value.
2. **Evaluate before training**, on iterations divisible by `eval_interval` (250 for the baby GPT) [`train.py:263-264`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L263-L264). Iteration 0 is evaluated too, which gives you the untrained loss; saving is skipped at iteration 0.
3. **Accumulate.** Each micro-step runs the forward pass under autocast, divides the loss, fetches the next batch, then runs backward [`train.py:292-305`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L292-L305). The fetch sits *between* forward and backward on purpose: the GPU is still busy with queued work, so the CPU's slicing costs nothing. With `gradient_accumulation_steps = 1`, as in the baby config, the loop runs once.
4. **Clip, then step.** Gradients are unscaled, their combined length is capped at 1.0, and AdamW updates the weights [`train.py:306-312`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L306-L312). Clipping before the step means one freak batch cannot throw the weights far.
5. **Free memory.** `zero_grad(set_to_none=True)` drops the gradient tensors instead of filling them with zeros [`train.py:314`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L314).
6. **Log.** Every `log_interval` iterations it prints loss, milliseconds and MFU. `loss.item()` makes the CPU wait for the GPU, so it only happens on log iterations [`train.py:320-323`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L320-L323).

What is *not* in the loop matters too. There are no epochs, no shuffling pass and no early stopping: it ends when `iter_num > max_iters` [`train.py:331-333`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L331-L333). Dropout stays on throughout; only `estimate_loss` switches the model to eval mode, and back again when it is done [`train.py:218-227`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L218-L227).

**Flow: One training iteration with gradient accumulation** (trigger: Each pass through the `while True:` loop in `train.py`.)

1. **Set this iteration's learning rate** [`train.py:257-260`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L257-L260) `get_lr` ramps up linearly for `warmup_iters`, then follows a cosine down to `min_lr` [`train.py:231-242`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L231-L242). The value is written into every parameter group.
2. **Every eval_interval: measure and save** [`train.py:262-288`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L262-L288) Only the main process does it. `estimate_loss` averages `eval_iters` random batches per split in eval mode [`train.py:214-228`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L214-L228), then a checkpoint may be written.
3. **Micro-step loop; DDP syncs only on the last one** [`train.py:292-298`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L292-L298) With DDP, gradients are averaged across GPUs only on the final micro-step, which saves all but one round of communication per iteration.
4. **Forward under autocast, divide the loss** [`train.py:299-301`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L299-L301) The forward pass runs in bfloat16/float16 where safe. Dividing by the number of micro-steps makes the summed gradients equal to the average over the big batch.
5. **Fetch the next batch while the GPU works** [`train.py:302-303`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L302-L303) GPU work is queued asynchronously, so the CPU slices the next batch from the memmap while the GPU is still busy.
6. **Backward, scaled for float16** [`train.py:304-305`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L304-L305) Gradients are added into each weight's `.grad`; repeating this over the micro-steps is the accumulation.
7. **Unscale and clip** [`train.py:306-309`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L306-L309) If the gradient vector is longer than 1.0 it is shrunk to length 1.0. Unscaling first means the threshold applies to the real gradients.
8. **AdamW step** [`train.py:310-312`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L310-L312) The optimizer built by `configure_optimizers` updates every weight [`model.py:280-284`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L280-L284); the scaler skips the step if float16 overflowed.
9. **Drop the gradients** [`train.py:313-314`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L313-L314) Setting them to `None` frees the memory until the next backward pass recreates them.
10. **Log loss, time and MFU** [`train.py:316-327`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L316-L327) The printed loss is the last micro-batch's loss multiplied back up, an approximation. MFU is smoothed over iterations after the first 5.
11. **Stop after max_iters** [`train.py:328-333`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L328-L333) There is no notion of epochs: training ends on an iteration count.

> **Checkpoint:** Why does `get_batch('train')` come between the forward pass and `backward()`?
> - `backward()` needs the next batch
> - The GPU is still working through the queued forward pass, so loading the next batch on the CPU overlaps with it and costs no extra time
> - To shuffle the data
> - DDP requires it
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>The GPU is still working through the queued forward pass, so loading the next batch on the CPU overlaps with it and costs no extra time. The comment says it: "immediately async prefetch next batch while model is doing the forward pass on the GPU" [`train.py:302-303`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L302-L303). Commit `3fd4c0c` puts the saving at "about 1ms lol".</details>

### Loading GPT-2's weights from Hugging Face

*standard · 6 min*

**In short:** `GPT.from_pretrained` builds an empty nanoGPT with GPT-2's exact shape, downloads OpenAI's checkpoint through `transformers`, and copies every tensor across by name, transposing the four kinds of weight OpenAI stored as Conv1D.

By the end you know why nanoGPT can load OpenAI's weights at all, and the one trick it needs.

It works because `model.py` copies GPT-2's design down to the parameter names: `transformer.h.0.attn.c_attn.weight` means the same tensor in both implementations, as do `ln_1`, `mlp.c_fc` and `lm_head`. The import is a dictionary walk, not a translation. Step through the flow below; these are the parts that need care.

**The shape is fixed by name.** You choose `gpt2`, `gpt2-medium`, `gpt2-large` or `gpt2-xl`, and that sets layers, heads and width [`model.py:216-221`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L216-L221). Vocabulary 50,257, context 1,024 and biases are forced, since that is how OpenAI trained them. Only dropout may be overridden [`model.py:209-211`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L209-L211).

**Not everything in a state dict is a weight.** Both sides contain attention-mask buffers (`.attn.bias`, `.attn.masked_bias`). They are filtered out, and then the two key counts must match exactly [`model.py:242-248`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L242-L248).

**The transpose.** OpenAI's original code used a `Conv1D` module that stores its weight as (in, out), while `nn.Linear` stores (out, in). For the four kinds of matrix that went through Conv1D, nanoGPT copies the transpose; everything else is copied as is, with a shape assertion on every tensor [`model.py:245-259`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/model.py#L245-L259).

**After loading.** `train.py` copies the forced values back into `model_args`, so a later `resume` rebuilds the right shape [`train.py:186-188`](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT/blob/3adf61e154c3fe3fca428ad6bc3818b27a3b8291/train.py#L186-L188), and it can shorten the context with `crop_block_size` if you asked for a smaller `block_size`.
